opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's useful to lay out the landscape, because people often lump these together when they're actually making very different bets.

At one end, you have what I'd call the purely neural approach: you train a large model, say a transformer, on huge amounts of code or structured data, and you sample programs from it. That has been remarkably successful. These models have absorbed an enormous amount of prior knowledge about what programs tend to look like, and they're very good at producing plausible-looking structure. But they generate token by token, and plausibility isn't the same as correctness. The model doesn't really have a notion of the semantics of what it's producing unless that's somehow implicitly learned, and you see the cracks when you push it out of distribution or ask for something that requires precise, multi-step reasoning.

At the other end, you have classical program synthesis: enumerative search, constraint solving, SMT-based approaches, deductive synthesis. These take the semantics seriously. You have a specification, a DSL, and you search a space of programs, checking whether each candidate actually satisfies the spec. The problem is that the space is combinatorially enormous, so unless your DSL is very carefully designed, search blows up. And the knowledge of what a "good" program looks like is mostly hand-engineered into the language and the search heuristics.

Then there's this big middle ground, which I find the most interesting: neurosymbolic or neurally guided search. You use a learned model as a proposal distribution or a heuristic, and you keep the symbolic machinery, an interpreter, a type checker, a verifier, in the loop to ground things. Work like DreamCoder is a nice example, where you're not just searching but also learning a library of abstractions over time, so the language itself grows. And now with LLMs, you see a lot of "generate and test" setups: sample many candidates, execute them, filter, refine.

The way I tend to frame it is in probabilistic terms. Program generation is inference. You have a prior over programs, you have some likelihood, how well does this program explain the data or satisfy the spec, and you want the posterior. Neural models give you a really rich prior and a fast amortized proposal. Symbolic execution gives you the likelihood, the actual grounding. Most of the interesting design questions are about how you combine those: Do you do sequential Monte Carlo over partial programs? Do you constrain decoding with a grammar or types? Do you do something more like Bayesian model refinement?

And the reason I care about this beyond code is that the same structure shows up everywhere we want models of the world: causal models, scientific hypotheses, simulators. Those are all compositional objects, and I think the question of how to generate them reliably, with real uncertainty and real grounding, is one of the central questions for building systems that can actually reason rather than just pattern-match.

r001.rationale: It contrasts purely neural learning from large example corpora with synthesis methods that use specifications, semantics, and symbolic checking, then places neurally guided search between them.

r002.rationale: It says the program space is combinatorially enormous and search can blow up, but does not identify often unbounded dimensionality as the reason searching is difficult.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd carve it up is that there are really three or four quite different traditions here, and they have very different assumptions baked into them, and I think the interesting question right now is how they're colliding.

So the oldest one, in a sense, is program synthesis coming out of programming languages and formal methods. There you typically have a specification, maybe a logical formula, maybe input-output examples, and you search over a space of programs in a domain-specific language until you find one that satisfies it. The emphasis is on correctness. You want something that you can prove meets the spec. And the search is often combinatorial, so a lot of the cleverness is in pruning the space, in using types, in using the structure of the language itself to cut things down. The downside is that those spaces are enormous and the methods tend to fall over once the programs get beyond a certain size, or once the specification isn't crisp.

Then you have the probabilistic programming and Bayesian program learning tradition, which is closer to where I come from. There you reframe the whole thing as inference. You say, there's a generative process that produces programs, there's a prior over programs, there's a likelihood that connects a program to the data you've observed, and finding a program is doing posterior inference. And I think what that framing buys you is a principled way to deal with uncertainty and with the fact that the data underdetermines the program. You're not looking for the one right answer, you're looking for a distribution. Things like DreamCoder sit somewhere in here, where you're also learning the library, learning the language itself, so the space you're searching over gets better over time.

And then the third tradition, which is obviously the dominant one at the moment, is just large neural models that have been trained on lots of code. And here the structure isn't explicit at all, or it's only implicit. You don't have a grammar, you don't have a search, you have a sequence model and it's learned the statistics of code well enough to produce things that are usually syntactically valid and often semantically reasonable. And that's remarkable, frankly. The thing those systems are bad at is exactly what the first two are good at, which is guarantees, and being able to say why a particular program was produced, and generalizing in a systematic way to things outside the training distribution.

So the way I think about it is in terms of where the compositionality lives. In the symbolic approaches, compositionality is in the representation. The program is built out of pieces, and the meaning of the whole is a function of the meaning of the parts, and that's what gives you systematic generalization. In the neural approaches, whatever compositionality there is has to be learned, and it's sort of smeared across the weights, and it's fragile in ways that are hard to predict.

And I think the most interesting work now, and what we're trying to do, is to not treat this as a choice. You can use a neural model as a proposal distribution, as a heuristic that guides a search or guides inference, while keeping the explicit program as the thing you're actually committing to. So the neural net gives you the good guesses, and the symbolic machinery gives you the structure, the ability to verify, the ability to compose things that have never been composed before. The hard part, and the part I think is genuinely unsolved, is doing that in a way where the two sides actually inform each other rather than just being bolted together, so that the program-level structure feeds back and shapes what the model learns, not just the other way around.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts explicit symbolic structure with neural patterns learned from code, but it presents these as distinct traditions rather than framing them along a spectrum of incorporated semantic knowledge versus learning from examples.

r002.rationale: It says program spaces are enormous and search is combinatorial, but does not identify often unbounded dimensionality of compositional structures as the difficulty.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few different axes here that are useful to separate. One is how you represent the thing you’re generating. Is it a sequence of tokens, a syntax tree, or a program with some explicit semantics? Another is how you search over that space. You might use a learned model, some kind of symbolic search, or a combination of the two.

Those choices aren’t necessarily in opposition. A neural network can propose a program, and then an interpreter can execute it to see whether it satisfies some specification. That gives you a different kind of feedback from simply asking whether the program looks like programs in your training data. You can ask whether it actually does what you wanted, at least on the cases you can check.

Of course, that pushes a lot of the difficulty into the specification. What does it mean to do what you wanted? If you give a few input-output examples, there are generally many programs consistent with them. So you still need some inductive bias—a preference for certain explanations or solutions over others. Learning can be very useful there, because it can guide you toward parts of the search space that would otherwise be difficult to find.

And with compositional structures, the attraction is that you can reuse pieces in new arrangements. But having a compositional representation doesn’t, by itself, mean your system will generalize compositionally. You also need a way to discover useful pieces and understand how their behavior changes when you put them together. So I’m interested in how learning, search, and execution can work together, rather than treating any one of those as the whole solution.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts learned proposals with symbolic search and execution-based feedback, but it does not frame approaches as a spectrum from semantic knowledge to learning purely from examples.

r002.rationale: It says many programs can fit examples and that search can be difficult, but does not identify the potentially unbounded dimensionality of compositional structures as a reason.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one useful way to look at it is to ask where the structure comes from. Is it something we build into the system, or is it something the system has to discover from data?

In program synthesis, for example, you might specify a language of programs and search for a program that satisfies some examples or a specification. That gives you a very explicit notion of composition: you have these pieces, and rules for putting them together. The difficulty is that the space of possible combinations becomes enormous very quickly.

With a neural approach, you can learn which combinations are plausible. You can generate a program in much the same way that you generate a sequence of words. But a program also has this additional property: you can execute it. So you don't just have to ask whether it looks like a good program; you can ask what it actually does.

And I think the interesting approaches combine those things. Learning can guide the search, and execution can provide feedback that constrains it. You might also learn new building blocks, so that something which initially required a long sequence of operations becomes a reusable component.

So, for me, the question isn't simply whether to use neural networks or symbolic methods. It's how to get a system that can propose structures, test them, and develop useful abstractions that make the next problem easier.

r001.rationale: It contrasts structure built into a system with structure learned from data, then illustrates the distinction with explicit program rules and neural learning from examples.

r002.rationale: It says the space of possible program combinations becomes enormous quickly, making search difficult.
